steps.prompt: Your model looks perfect in Blender. Will it look right in Unity?
steps.sub: Not automatically. Getting a model across cleanly is a small pipeline: export the right file, import it, fix materials, add a collider. By the end you'll run that pipeline in order.

steps.prompt: First instinct — how does a Blender model reach Unity?

options.t: Save the .blend file and open it directly as the game.
Export to a shared 3D format like FBX or GLTF, then import that file into Unity.
Take a screenshot of the model and drag the image in.

steps.why: Tools talk through interchange formats. Blender exports FBX or GLTF — formats Unity understands — and you drop that file into Unity's project. A screenshot is flat (no 3D), and a raw .blend isn't how you ship assets into a clean pipeline.
hints: Unity can't read Blender's native brain — it needs a shared language.
FBX and GLTF are the two common 'everyone understands me' 3D formats.

steps.prompt: What actually travels across — and what doesn't.
steps.sub: Tap each card. These are the four things to get right.

cards.b: The geometry itself — the shape, the vertices. This crosses over reliably in FBX/GLTF.
The image files (color, normal, roughness). They often DON'T auto-embed — you may import them and re-link.
How the surface looks. Blender's material may not survive — you rebuild it on Unity's shader.
An invisible shape Unity adds so the model can collide. It is NOT in the model — you add it in Unity.

steps.prompt: Where does each thing get handled?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then tap the tool where you do it.

items.t: Apply scale and rotation so the model isn't sideways
Add a Box Collider so the player can stand on it
Re-link the texture images to the material
Make sure the export includes UVs and the mesh
Assign the material to Unity's Standard shader

hints: Anything about preparing or exporting the model happens in Blender first.
Colliders, shader hookup, and re-linking textures are all done after the model is inside Unity.

steps.prompt: You imported the model. It's there — but solid magenta / hot pink. What does that mean?
steps.sub: Pink is Unity's universal 'something's wrong' color.

options.t: The mesh failed to import and there's no geometry.
The material can't find its texture or shader — the link is broken.
The model is too big for Unity to render.

steps.why: Magenta is Unity's missing-material flag: the mesh is fine, but the material has no working shader/texture. The fix is in the Unity pipeline — assign a shader (e.g. Standard) and re-link the texture maps. It's the single most common import surprise.
hints: If the SHAPE is visible, the mesh imported fine — so it's not geometry.
Pink in Unity almost always points at the material, not the mesh.

steps.prompt: Tap the import pipeline steps in the right order.
steps.sub: From a finished Blender model to a model that behaves in the scene.
chips: In Unity, fix the material and re-link textures
Export the model from Blender as FBX/GLTF
Add a collider so it interacts physically
Drag the exported file into Unity's project
hints: It can't be in Unity before it leaves Blender.
Get it in, make it look right, then make it solid.

steps.prompt: Walk a real model — a treasure chest — through the pipeline.
steps.sub: At each turn, pick the right next move. The log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Get the chest into Unity looking right and standing on the floor.

turns.situation: The chest is modelled in Blender. It's leaning 15° because you rotated it while building.
turns.q: Before exporting, what's the smart first move?
options: Apply the rotation so its 'rest' pose is upright
Export it leaning — fix it later in Unity
turns.log: 🎨 Applied transforms → chest sits upright at zero rotation.

turns.situation: The chest is clean. You need it in Unity.
options: Export as FBX/GLTF, then drag that file into Unity
turns.log: 📦 Exported chest.fbx → dragged into Unity project.

turns.situation: It appears in the scene — but it's solid magenta.
turns.q: What's going on, and what do you do?
options: Material link is broken — assign a shader and re-link its texture
Unity is broken — restart the computer
turns.log: 🎨 Assigned Standard shader + re-linked wood texture → chest looks right.

turns.situation: The chest looks great, but the player walks straight through it.
options: A collider — add one so it's physically solid
A second copy of the chest
turns.log: 🧱 Added Box Collider → player can stand on the chest. Done.

hints: The pipeline order is: prep → export/import → fix material → add collider.
Magenta = material. Walk-through = no collider. Each symptom maps to one step.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: Exporting from Blender always carries the materials over perfectly into Unity.
statements.why: No — materials and textures often need rebuilding or re-linking in Unity. The mesh travels reliably; the look frequently doesn't.

statements.t: A model with no collider will be visible but not physically solid.
statements.why: Right — without a collider the player and physics pass straight through it. Visuals and physics are separate.

statements.t: FBX and GLTF are formats both Blender and Unity understand.
statements.why: Yes — they're interchange formats made for moving 3D assets between tools.

statements.t: If you forget to apply scale in Blender, your model can import wildly too big or tiny.
statements.why: True — unapplied scale carries strange numbers across, so the chest might import 100× too large. Applying transforms first avoids it.

hints: Remember which things cross reliably (mesh) and which don't (materials/textures).
Visible and solid are two different problems with two different fixes.

steps.sub: Not graded. Picture importing one asset from YOUR game idea.

fields.label: Which asset will you import first?
fields.ph: e.g. my robot enemy / the treasure key / the spaceship

fields.label: How will you know the import worked?
fields.ph: e.g. it shows the right texture AND the player can't walk through it

steps.prompt: Last check — which order avoids the most pain?
steps.sub: One ordering catches problems early; the others find them too late.

options.t: Add the collider in Blender, then never touch materials.
Prep in Blender → import → fix materials → add collider, testing after each.
Import everything at once, ship it, and fix whatever players report.

steps.why: Prep first, bring it in, make it look right, then make it solid — testing at each step means you know exactly which stage broke when something's off. Colliders aren't a Blender export, and shipping untested invites the magenta-and-fall-through bugs to surface in front of players.
hints: You want the smallest possible gap between 'I changed something' and 'I saw if it worked'.
Colliders are a Unity step, not a Blender one.
